title: Smelter-at-the-dam siting: fab beside U.S. helium-rich gas fields
idea: Adapted from aluminum smelters built next to hydro dams: site a U.S. DRAM fab near helium-rich gas processing (Kansas Hugoton, Texas Panhandle, Wyoming LaBarge) with a dedicated helium extraction and liquefaction take piped straight to the fab and cheap gas-fired power.
why: Makes helium supply independent of Qatar and fully domestic, and pairs it with low-cost energy; fab helium becomes a fixed-cost utility (scarce resources, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Magnify the die to a whole undiced wafer slab
idea: Skip dicing, packaging and per-die final test: ship whole 300 mm DRAM wafers with fuse-mapped redundancy, face-to-face bonded to a wafer-scale logic or interposer wafer as a rack 'memory slab'.
why: Packaging, test and singulation are ~15-25% of DRAM cost and HBM TSV yield loss is 20-30%; a wafer slab avoids both while giving huge bandwidth.

title: Garden hose: R2R embossed polymer waveguide sheets for rack memory pooling
idea: Random stimulus 'garden hose' -> cheap flexible pipes carry flow anywhere. R2R hot-embossed polymer optical waveguide sheets are laminated into racks as passive optical backplanes for CXL memory pooling, at a fraction of fiber-harness cost.
why: Pooling cuts per-server DRAM over-provisioning ~10-25%, a direct gain in usable supply, at ~1-2 pJ/bit links.

title: Rack memory spot exchange auctioning stranded GB-hours over CXL
idea: Worse: let every server own its memory so 25-50% sits stranded while neighbors swap to disk. Flip: a rack-level CXL switch pools DRAM and a scheduler runs a sub-second auction in which tenants bid for GB-hours, publishing the clearing price as an internal scarcity signal.
why: Cuts cluster DRAM provisioning ~20-30% for the same workloads, equivalent to new supply with no fab.

title: Child asks why servers don't share: per-second rack memory market
idea: A child sees half of each server's RAM sitting idle and asks why they don't share. A CXL 3.x rack pool lends each host's stranded DRAM in 256 MB slices through a per-second internal auction run by the fabric manager, and reclaims a slice in under 100 ms by migrating its pages to a compressed tier.
why: Usable supply: hyperscaler DRAM utilization is ~50-60%; pooling plus a price signal could cut fleet DRAM purchases 15-25%, at ~200 ns extra latency on borrowed pages.

title: ScaleMP's software DSM fixed: CXL-switched rack memory pool
idea: ScaleMP's vSMP (software distributed shared memory across servers) faded because network latency made remote pages slow and fragile. Fix: pool memory in hardware with a CXL switch shelf, where each server borrows 1 GB slices at ~250-400 ns under a fabric manager and returns them when jobs end.
why: Usable supply: clouds strand ~25-30% of server DRAM unused; pooling can cut fleet DRAM purchases by ~10-15%.

title: Lichen pairing: DRAM fab fused with a domestic helium gas plant
idea: Lichen fuses an alga and a fungus into one organism that thrives where neither could alone. Site a DRAM fab beside a U.S. natural-gas helium separation plant (e.g., Hugoton field), taking captive helium by pipeline and using the plant's cryogenic cold for fab chillers in exchange for long-term offtake.
why: Removes exposure to Qatar helium (~30% of supply, offline) and cuts chiller energy ~10-20%.

title: Import wafers, onshore the dry end: U.S. memory finishing hub
idea: Rearrange where value is added: the U.S. imports finished DRAM wafers from allied fabs. It onshores the high-value, low-water steps: thinning, TSV reveal, hybrid bonding, HBM stacking, CXL module build and test.
why: The back end uses about an order of magnitude less water per wafer than the front end. It gives the U.S. a fast foothold in HBM/CXL supply without a 3-5 year front-end build.

title: Circadian coupled-oscillator phase memory in standard logic
idea: Circadian clocks store time of day as the phase of a biochemical oscillator. Bits are stored as the 0 or 180 degree phase of sub-harmonically injection-locked ring oscillators (parametron-style), built only from logic transistors with no capacitor.
why: Memory any logic fab can make with its standard design rules; trades standby power for refresh-free retention.

title: Nacre brick-and-mortar: ALD-stacked capacitorless oxide tiers
idea: Nacre gets its strength from hundreds of thin mineral tiles bonded by organic layers. Monolithic stacks of 50-100 tiers of capacitorless oxide-TFT cells are deposited by low-temperature ALD, then patterned once with a staircase and vertical access holes, like 3D NAND with no capacitor in any tier.
why: Density comes from tiers rather than EUV, on more available NAND-style tooling; gets around the 3D DRAM capacitor blocker.

title: Core-Rope ROM for Frozen Model Weights in Mature Fabs
idea: Revive Apollo's core rope memory, where the program was woven into the hardware: frozen foundation-model weights are written into via-programmed multi-level ROM chiplets (one custom via mask per model on a 28-40 nm mature line), read with small-swing sensing and no refresh or row restore, stacked beside the accelerator.
why: Energy per access ~10x lower than DRAM (~0.3 pJ/bit, no activation, restore or refresh); frees the large share of inference DRAM that only holds static weights, using mature-fab capacity.

title: Legacy-socket emulator: one modern chip impersonates four obsolete ones
idea: 30-year industrial and avionics users hoard obsolete SDRAM and EDO. A 10-person firm builds pin-compatible carrier boards where a small FPGA plus one modern LPDDR4 chip emulates the old parts' timing exactly, releasing hoarded die banks and mature-node wafer starts.
why: Removes legacy demand on mature capacity; the lesson that generalizes is to decouple the interface from the die.

title: Anamartic Wafer Stack redux: self-configuring wafer-scale memory slabs
idea: Ivor Catt's Anamartic wafer-scale memory (1989) chained good dies on an uncut wafer into a spiral but died because hand-assembled wafer stacks could not keep up with falling DRAM die prices. Fix with 1990s tools only: on fully depreciated 200 mm, 180 nm lines, pattern whole wafers of DRAM tiles with built-in self-test that fuses a spiral chain through good tiles, and ship each wafer as one memory slab with no dicing, die packaging or per-die sort.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: uses zero-book tools in idle 200 mm fabs and removes packaging and test (~25-35% of module cost); ~5-7 GB per 200 mm wafer, so it is surge capacity, not a cost-per-bit leader.

title: 2021 PMIC choke fixed: domestic old-node lines for DIMM companions
idea: DDR5 module output was throttled in 2021-22 by a shortage of power-management ICs, and Japan's Minimal Fab (half-inch wafers) struggled for lack of a killer product. Fix: dedicate small domestic 200 mm and Minimal-Fab-style lines (0.18-0.5 um BCD, 1990s-class) to the simple chips every module needs (PMIC, SPD hub, temperature sensor), with buyer-funded buffer inventory.
why: Supply resilience: a $2 chip should never block a $500 module; this removes a chokepoint that has already limited DDR5 module output.

title: Phones feed servers: robotic LPDDR harvesting from e-waste
idea: Reverse the e-waste flow: robots desolder LPDDR packages from recycled phones and laptops with hot gas. The packages are re-balled with dry flux, tested and mounted on CAMM/SOCAMM-style CXL or edge-inference boards.
why: Huge numbers of GB sit in discarded devices. Harvested capacity uses no fab water and only dry rework, so water per usable GB is >100x lower than for new bits.

title: Fab sells heat, not steam: district heating replaces cooling towers
idea: Reverse waste into product: heat pumps raise fab heat to 70-90 C and sell it to city district heating and greenhouses. Dry coolers reject the rest, and the evaporative cooling towers are retired.
why: Cooling towers evaporate a large share of a fab's water. Selling heat and rejecting the rest dry cuts evaporative loss >10x, and the heat revenue offsets the cost.

title: Scatter-hoard strategic DRAM reserve with rotating stock
idea: Jays and squirrels scatter caches across many sites and eat the oldest first. A national or consortium reserve buys DRAM in price troughs, holds it in many distributed bonded warehouses, and rotates stock into government and education systems every ~18 months so it never goes obsolete; releases trigger automatically when contract prices pass a set multiple.
why: Damps 4x price spikes and secures critical supply; rotation limits holding cost to inventory carry instead of write-offs.

title: Papermaker's book: roll-to-roll foil memory laminated 800 sheets deep
idea: A papermaker makes thick books from cheap sheets. Print single-tier oxide-TFT gain-cell memory on 10 um polyimide foil by roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~100 nm rules, then laminate ~800 sheets per cm with anisotropic conductive film and edge-plated through-stack bus lines into a memory 'book'.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: ~60 MB/cm^2 per sheet times 800 sheets is ~50 GB/cm^3, versus ~2 GB/cm^3 for a DIMM. Roll-to-roll costs (~$20-50/m^2 per sheet) keep cost per module flat; sheet alignment and yield are the risks.

title: Die-transplant repair rebuilds DIMMs with one failed die
idea: Box[Source=RMA'd DIMMs x Transform=localized hot-gas rework swapping single failed DRAM packages x Integration=standard DDR5 DIMM x Owner=repair depot]: most failed DIMMs lose one of 10-20 packages; replace just that package with a harvested good one and requalify, instead of scrapping 19 good dies.
why: Raises yield of the installed base: recovers ~95% of bits in failed modules; unchanged DDR interface.

title: Diablo's litigation death: buyer fund buys orphaned memory patents
idea: Diablo Technologies' Memory1 died after patent litigation drained it, while orphaned portfolios from Qimonda, Elpida, Spansion and others went to patent assertion entities. Fix: a defensive patent fund financed by memory buyers acquires distressed memory portfolios at auction, grants royalty-free licenses to members' suppliers, and offers litigation cover to new entrants.
why: Lowers the legal risk and royalty load that has sunk memory startups, making it cheaper for new DRAM-class suppliers to enter.

title: Copy-exactly DRAM micro-fab franchise replicated across states
idea: Worse: build one $15B gigafab every five years in one place. Flip: design a standardized ~10k wafers/month DRAM module (fixed tool set, recipes, building) and franchise it to regional operators who pay royalties while the franchisor runs centralized yield engineering and tool spares.
why: Entry ticket falls to ~$2-3B per site, capacity arrives in small staggered steps and U.S. manufacturing spreads out.

title: Substitute new fabs with bolt-on memory-tier upfit shops
idea: Swap greenfield fabs for independent BEOL-only upfit shops (no implant, no furnaces above 400 C) that receive customers' finished logic or DRAM wafers and deposit extra memory tiers on top, like a paint shop for wafers.
why: Capex ~$1-2B versus $15B+, buildable in ~18 months; adds bits to wafers that already exist.

title: Polysilicon capacitor mold etched with HBr and stripped by TMAH
idea: Combine a thick doped-polysilicon storage-node mold (etched to high AR with HBr/O2 cryogenic etch) with ALD electrode and dielectric deposition and a wet TMAH mold strip, replacing the C4F6/C4F8 high-AR oxide mold etch.
why: Removes the costliest fluorocarbon etch step in DRAM while keeping 1T1C capacitors, and silicon etch may reach higher AR than oxide.

title: Anodized alumina pore arrays as self-organized capacitor molds
idea: Fuse industrial aluminum anodizing (oxalic/phosphoric acid, guided by an imprinted seed pattern) with DRAM capacitor fabrication. Self-ordered hexagonal AAO pores with AR over 100:1 become the storage-node mold, lined by ALD TiN, ZrO2 and TiN.
why: Delivers AR of about 115 (the Cs wall), skips EUV and fluorocarbon etch for the capacitor layer, and uses anodizing tools that cost pennies per wafer.

title: Substitute fab-owned tools with an aircraft-style lithography leasing bank
idea: Swap each fab buying its own scanners and etchers for a sovereign-backed lessor (AerCap-style) that owns tool fleets, leases them by wafer-hour and moves them between fabs as the cycle turns.
why: Attacks capital intensity: depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; higher fleet use and cheaper lessor capital could cut tool cost per wafer ~15-25% and let new entrants start without $15B.

title: Never break vacuum: cluster-continuous fab without wet benches
idea: Rearrange the fab from a hall of separate tools to linked vacuum clusters: wafers stay under vacuum between deposition, etch and in-situ cleans (anhydrous HF vapor, remote H2/NH3 plasma). Native oxide and particles never form, so the wet bench between steps goes away.
why: Removes the cleans and rinses caused by queue time, cutting UPW >10x on those modules. It also shortens cycle time and shrinks the cleanroom.

title: Deli slicer: roll-to-roll exfoliated silicon foils multiply wafers per boule
idea: Random stimulus 'deli slicer' -> thin slices from one log. Ion-cut/spalling exfoliates 10-20 um crystalline silicon layers from a reusable CZ donor, and roller-based transfer lays them onto temperature-tolerant ceramic carrier tape for device processing.
why: One boule yields ~10x more device substrates, cutting HPQ crucible and polysilicon use per bit ~10x and kerf loss to zero.

title: Catt Spiral Revival: Wafer-Scale Memory From Rejected DRAM Wafers
idea: Revive Ivor Catt's 1989 Anamartic self-organizing spiral wafer: instead of dicing rejected or partial-yield DRAM wafers, probe-map every die, bond a small harvest-controller chiplet per reticle field, and let a boot-time 'spiral' protocol chain only the good dies into a serial-linked string that a host sees as one wafer-scale CXL memory slab of 100-300 GB.
why: Scarce-resource and cost per bit: salvages wafers and dies now scrapped or down-binned for a few defects (plus HBM-stack yield losses of 20-30%); claimed +5-10% effective bit supply at near-zero capex.

title: Par-baked wafer bank with late product differentiation
idea: Like bakeries that par-bake bread and finish to order, fabs stop wafers after the cell array and capacitor (the long FEOL), park them, then finish BEOL and test as DDR5, LPDDR5 or HBM core die only when orders arrive.
why: Cuts the effective response time from ~16 weeks to ~6 and lets one wafer pool serve whichever product is short, reducing mismatch waste and panic double-ordering.

title: Memory passports: certified pre-owned DRAM exchange with telemetry
idea: Rearrange the market: every module logs ECC corrections, temperature and activation counts to a 'passport' kept in its SPD. A clearinghouse grades and warrants used memory from that history, so it trades like a certified pre-owned car.
why: Lack of trust blocks reuse. Warrantied second-life memory adds capacity with >10x less water per GB than new fab output.

title: Mechanics substitution: maskless multi-beam write for the single added layer
idea: TRIZ #28 Replace mechanical system: the one permitted extra litho layer is written by multi-beam e-beam direct write instead of a physical photomask, letting micro-fabs personalize DRAM (repair, config, customer ID) per wafer with no mask shop.
why: Capital: removes ~$1-3M mask cost and mask-shop lead time for small-volume DRAM fabs.

title: Phase transition: reworkable HBM via one-mask low-melt sacrificial bond layer
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: one mask defines a low-melting indium/thermoplastic sacrificial ring at each core-die interface so a stack with a failing layer can be locally reheated, split and re-stacked with a good die.
why: HBM yield loss 20-30%: rework recovers most stacks instead of scrapping 11 good dies.

title: IBM System/360 Channel Programs Run Inside the Memory Module
idea: Revive the 1964 S/360 I/O channel, which executed its own channel-command-word programs: CXL memory modules accept CCW-style scatter, gather, filter and top-k programs, walk pointers locally, and return only result bytes to the host.
why: Data movement and overfetch: for pointer chasing, KV lookups and embeddings, 10-100x fewer bits cross the link, >=10x lower energy per useful access, and one module serves more hosts.

title: Substitute monolithic DRAM fabs with split array fab plus logic-foundry periphery
idea: Swap making periphery in the DRAM fab for buying periphery wafers from idle U.S. mature-logic foundries and hybrid-bonding them face-to-face onto array-only wafers made in a lean array fab.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; moving it to existing logic capacity frees ~40% more array area per DRAM wafer and lets the U.S. use fabs it already has.

title: IBM 650 SOAP Revival: Time-Placing Tensors so Flash Replaces DRAM
idea: Revive the 1955 Symbolic Optimal Assembly Program, which placed each instruction on the drum so it arrived under the read head just when needed: a compiler for static AI graphs lays out every weight and KV block across NAND/SSD stripes so it streams in just in time through a small DRAM staging ring.
why: Usable supply: replaces most resident-weight DRAM with flash at ~10-20x lower cost per bit; DRAM per served model can drop 5-10x.

title: Rail yard master: racetrack memory built in U.S. hard-disk head fabs
idea: A rail yard master moves cars along sidings instead of building a track for each car. Magnetic domain-wall racetrack memory uses vertical U-shaped nanowires, each holding ~64 domains shifted by current past one read/write head. It is built in U.S. hard-disk read-head fabs, which already pattern 20 nm magnetic multilayers in volume and are losing HDD demand.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 bits per ~4F^2 track footprint is ~10-20x DRAM areal density. The head fabs are depreciated, domain-wall motion does not wear out, and shift latency is tens of ns; pinning and shift errors are the risks.

title: FB-DIMM's hot buffer fixed: off-path refresh-brain rescues weak dies
idea: FB-DIMM's advanced memory buffer died of heat (several watts) because it sat in the data path. Fix: keep a 180 nm buffer off the data path and use it only for control: it profiles each row's retention at boot and drives multi-rate refresh (RAIDR-style), refreshing strong rows rarely and weak rows often.
why: Refresh: cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss by ~50-75%, and lets dies rejected for a few short-retention rows ship as standard parts.

title: Ti: Rutile TiO2 on tin-oxide seed breaks the capacitor charge wall
idea: Replace ZrO2-based capacitor dielectrics with rutile TiO2 (k ~80-100) crystallized at low temperature on an isostructural rutile SnO2 seed instead of scarce RuO2, with Ti precursor from U.S. ilmenite sands.
why: k ~90 meets the fact-sheet k~70 target, allowing ~40:1 instead of 75:1 pillars (cheaper etch, more cell headroom) and less Hf/Zr reliance.

title: Retention-map fingerprints certify provenance of reused DRAM
idea: Box[Sensing=read-back after controlled refresh pause x Transform=weak-cell retention map as physical unclonable fingerprint x Owner=neutral registry x Channel=secondary market]: each die's retention-failure map is a unique fingerprint, readable through standard DDR commands, logged in a registry to defeat counterfeit and remarked used DRAM.
why: Enables trusted second-life supply at scale; no interface change.

title: Cookie cutter: printed long-lead fab tool parts cut ramp time
idea: Random stimulus 'cookie cutter' -> shape on demand from stock. Regional additive-manufacturing farms print showerheads, gas manifolds, ESC bases and ceramic chamber liners by laser powder-bed fusion and binder-jet ceramics on demand.
why: Tool lead times of 12-18 months gate fab ramps; printed parts cut months off tool delivery and spares, pulling new DRAM capacity in earlier.

title: Bioreactor scale-out: clone container-sized memory fab cells
idea: Vaccine makers scale out with many identical single-use bioreactor trains instead of one giant tank. Build DRAM capacity as identical 1k-wafer/month 'fab cells'. Every tool sits in a sealed FOUP/SMIF minienvironment inside a prefabricated, container-scale cleanroom shell, and a cell is qualified once and then cloned in months.
why: Capital and time: removes the $1-2B ballroom cleanroom shell. Capacity lands in 9-12 months in small increments that can follow price cycles.

title: Etch metal, don't polish it: subtractive molybdenum wiring
idea: Reverse damascene (etch trench, plate, polish) into subtractive patterning: deposit a blanket molybdenum film by dry PVD/CVD and plasma-etch it into lines. That removes copper plating, metal CMP and their cleans, and Mo also replaces tungsten in contacts.
why: Removing plating baths and metal CMP cuts metallization water >10x. Molybdenum from U.S. mines also bypasses China's ~80% tungsten chokepoint.

title: Fab-in-a-factory: mass-produce identical modular DRAM fab bays
idea: Wright's law cuts cost ~20% per doubling, but every fab is bespoke construction built once. Design a standardized 2.5k-wafer/month fab module (cleanroom, sub-fab, utilities, tool set) prefabricated in a factory and shipped as ~40 truckable blocks, so each additional fab rides a learning curve.
why: Capital and time: after ~10 units construction cost falls ~50% and build time drops to 12-18 months versus 3-5 years.

title: Magnify levels 256x: 8-bit analog cells with neural sensing
idea: Store 8 bits per gain cell as an analog charge level written by closed-loop program-verify and read by a tiny on-chip learned ADC that tracks drift and leakage, built as 8 stacked BEOL oxide layers in a depreciated 200 mm fab.
why: 8 bits/cell x 8 layers = 64x bits per area on ~10x cheaper wafers, targeting ~100x lower $/GB while trading latency (~0.5-1 us) and energy.

title: Open-source mature-node DRAM PDK and cell library
idea: Follow open hardware such as the open SkyWater 130 PDK: publish an open trench- or stack-capacitor DRAM cell, sense amp and periphery IP on a 40-28 nm specialty-foundry flow under a permissive license, so foundries and startups can make merchant DRAM without licensing their way through the incumbents' patents.
why: Lowers the entry barrier, adds independent suppliers and raises U.S. manufacturability.

title: MLCC tape-stacking: hundred-layer horizontal capacitors contacted by one trench
idea: Copy multilayer ceramic capacitors. Sputter 20-50 alternating layers of electrode metal A (TiN) and metal B (W or Ru) separated by high-k. Etch one cell trench, then selectively recess A on one wall and B on the other so each fill touches only its own electrode set. The result is an interdigitated capacitor that scales with layer count, not aspect ratio.
why: Capacitor charge wall: 30 layers x ~0.5 fF gives ~15 fF with no AR-115 holes. Sputter, ALD and one etch are nanofab-standard.

title: Movable-type reticles: a shared library of standard array masks
idea: Gutenberg's movable type let one cast set be recombined into endless pages. Standardize the costliest array-layer reticles (active, buried wordline, bitline, storage node) as a licensed shared library. Each product or new entrant then designs and buys only its periphery and metal reticles.
why: Masks and capital: cuts per-product mask spend ~50-60% and design cycles ~6 months, lowering the entry barrier for second-source and micro-fab DRAM.

title: Ever-Normal Granary for Bits: Strategic DRAM Wafer Buffer Stock
idea: Revive the 1930s ever-normal granary and the Cold War National Defense Stockpile for memory: a government corporation buys finished, tested DRAM wafers in die-bank form (stored under dry nitrogen) during gluts at floor prices and sells them into shortages, holding about three months of national demand.
why: Supply volatility: shaves 4x price spikes and keeps fabs at full utilization in busts, lowering cost per bit ~10-15% over the cycle.

title: Bolt-of-cloth die: seamless tile fabric diced to any capacity
idea: Textile mills weave continuous bolts that are cut to any length. Lay out the wafer as a seamless sea of self-contained memory tiles, each with local periphery and a bus that crosses scribe lines. The saw then cuts any rectangle, so wafer-edge and defect-adjacent regions become smaller-capacity parts instead of scrap.
why: Usable area: recovers ~5-8% of the wafer lost to edge exclusion and partial dies, and one mask set serves many capacities.

title: Strontium-titanate capacitor on strontium-vanadate electrodes cuts aspect ratio threefold
idea: The charge wall says more charge needs k~70 or AR~115; thin-film SrTiO3 (k~150-300) clears it but historically needed Ru or Pt electrodes. Use SrVO3, a correlated-metal perovskite made of Sr, V and O, as a lattice-matched electrode to grow low-leakage STO at AR ~20:1.
why: Capacitor wall and capital: shorter capacitors remove the hardest HAR etch steps with no Ru; risks are small-gap leakage and crystallization thermal budget.

title: Retired AI GPUs reborn as networked HBM memory appliances
idea: Ideal: HBM never leaves service. Closest achievable with no new fab: when A100/H100 fleets retire, keep the boards in chassis as networked HBM servers (80 GB at TB/s each) that export KV-cache and embedding tables over RDMA to new accelerators.
why: Reuse of the costliest bits (3x wafer area per bit): billions of dollars of HBM stay in use 3-5 more years.

title: Two-gas fab: only on-site nitrogen and electrolytic hydrogen
idea: Fab-scale utilities redesign: every process is qualified to run on nitrogen made on site by pressure-swing adsorption, hydrogen and oxygen from water electrolysis, plus process chemicals. There is no bulk rare-gas yard, tank or delivery contract.
why: A rare-gas outage cannot shut the fab, and gas logistics and storage capex fall. It makes U.S. siting independent of noble-gas supply chains.

title: RepRap for nanofabs: open-hardware, self-replicating memory process tools
idea: RepRap 3D printers print their own parts. Publish open designs for a memory micro-fab's core tools (ALD reactor, sputter, mask aligner, RTA, wet benches) that a university nanofab and machine shop can build and copy, including fixtures each tool makes for the next.
why: Capital and time: drops a pilot memory line's tool bill from ~$50M to ~$3-5M, so dozens of regional micro-fabs can prototype and make niche memory.

title: Depreciated-node bit arbitrage via 2DPC low-density DIMMs
idea: Box[Source=fully depreciated 1y/1z lines x Medium=16 Gb DDR5 die x Integration=standard 2-DIMM-per-channel boards x Owner=DRAM maker + platform OEM]: keep depreciated lines on cheap 16 Gb DDR5 rather than converting them, and design platforms with 2DPC slots to reach capacity with lower-density DIMMs.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so depreciated-line bits can be ~30-40% cheaper despite lower density; standard DDR5.

title: Synthetic fused-silica crucibles replacing Spruce Pine quartz
idea: Po: crucibles are made, not mined. Czochralski crucibles are slip-cast from synthetic silica made by flame hydrolysis of domestic SiCl4 (a polysilicon byproduct), with a barium-doped inner layer that mimics natural high-purity quartz devitrification behavior.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine chokepoint for the wafers DRAM is built on and recycles a polysilicon waste stream; attacks scarce-resource intensity.

title: No wafer consumed: remote epitaxy on a reusable donor
idea: Forced limit: the substrate may not be used up. Crystalline Ge or InGaZnO-class films are grown by remote epitaxy through graphene on a donor that is reused 50 or more times, peeled off, and laminated onto glass or metal carriers.
why: Substrate consumption per device drops by about 50x, which decouples memory output from wafer and crucible supply.

title: Coelacanth revival: restart crosspoint lines for selector-only memory
idea: The coelacanth was thought extinct until it reappeared. Shuttered 3D crosspoint tooling is restarted for chalcogenide selector-only memory, which stores the bit as a threshold shift in the OTS itself, as a cheap DRAM-extension tier.
why: Reuses existing U.S. crosspoint know-how and tools; stacked 4F2 with no capacitor, at ~1/3 the cost per bit of DRAM.

title: Double tool maintenance intervals, absorbing drift-induced cell faults
idea: Inverts 'tools must always run at peak cleanliness': etch and deposition chambers run ~2x longer between wet cleans and seasoning, letting particle- and drift-induced single-cell defects climb toward the 1% budget, mapped out at test.
why: Capital intensity: equipment uptime rises ~8-15%, which is new capacity without new tools.

title: Hard-disk bit-patterned-media self-assembly for DRAM capacitor honeycombs
idea: Adapted from the HDD industry's block-copolymer work on bit-patterned media: a coarse guide pattern from a U.S.-built stepper plus a high-chi block copolymer from U.S. chemistry makers self-assembles the hexagonal storage-node hole array at ~20 nm pitch.
why: The capacitor array is the periodic hexagonal lattice BCPs form naturally, so this removes 1-2 EUV or SAQP layers with no ASML dependence for that layer (litho capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly of capacitor-hole arrays guided by UV-LED prepattern
idea: Scale jump from optics to molecules: polymer chains self-organize into a hexagonal array at 20-30 nm pitch, guided by a coarse prepattern exposed with 365 nm LED arrays rather than mercury-argon lamps or excimer lasers.
why: Patterns the densest DRAM layer without neon, argon or krypton light sources. Saves 2-4 EUV or multi-patterning steps per wafer.

title: Legacy-demand evacuation to depreciated lines under assurance contracts
idea: Worse: keep automotive, industrial and DDR4 demand on leading-edge lines so cars and AI fight for the same wafers. Flip: move all low-density demand to fully depreciated 2x-nm DRAM lines and U.S. mature foundries under 10-year 'legacy assurance' contracts that explicitly free leading-edge wafer starts.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so legacy bits cost about half on depreciated lines, releasing an estimated 10-15% of leading-edge capacity for dense parts.

title: Spheroidality: 1 mm spherical-silicon memory micro-fab processed inside tubes
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: drop-tower-grown 1 mm silicon spheres roll through sealed tubes for clean, deposit, expose (spherical-mirror litho) and etch, then are clustered into memory modules; no ingots, crucibles or ballroom cleanrooms.
why: Capital and crucible chokepoints: a tube-fab could cost ~1/10 per wafer-equivalent, though density per sphere is limited.

title: Physically delivered DRAM bit futures exchange to end hoarding
idea: Worse: keep pricing opaque and contract-only so OEMs panic-buy and hoard. Flip: list standardized monthly futures on a gigabit of DDR5-class known-good die with physical delivery from bonded warehouses, so buyers hedge price instead of stockpiling and fabs pre-sell future output to fund capex.
why: Releases hidden buffer inventory (plausibly 5-10% of annual supply) and lowers fab cost of capital via forward sales.

title: Ge: Shared silicon-germanium superlattice epi foundry for 3D DRAM
idea: A U.S. epi-as-a-service foundry grows 30-100-tier Si/SiGe superlattices, the starting stack for lateral 3D DRAM, on customer wafers using SiGe BiCMOS epi know-how, so new entrants need no epi capex.
why: 3D DRAM needs 26+ tiers and epi uniformity is a bottleneck; pooled tools cut entry capital and accelerate many 3D DRAM teams.

title: Orphan Drug Act incentives for U.S. legacy DRAM production
idea: Adapted from orphan-drug exclusivity and tax credits: give a U.S. maker 7-year exclusivity on federal procurement plus a 25% production credit for end-of-life DRAM types (DDR3/DDR4, LPDDR4, SDR) used in defense, auto, medical and industrial systems.
why: Secures parts for long-lived U.S. systems, lets incumbents move capacity to the leading edge, and gives a U.S. entrant a protected DUV starter market (U.S. manufacturability, supply).

title: Solar PVEL-style bankability scorecard for memory reliability
idea: Like the independent PV module scorecard that made new panel makers financeable, an independent lab buys parts off the line and publishes 125 C/10-year HTOL, retention and electromigration scores for every supplier, which lenders use as covenants.
why: Turns reliability into a public, bankable metric, cutting cost of capital for new fabs that score well and widening the supplier base.

title: Qimonda trench resurrected in MEMS DRIE fabs: 100 fF cells
idea: Qimonda's deep-trench DRAM lost because trenches could not shrink below ~50 nm. At 180 nm and above, shrinking does not matter: Bosch deep reactive-ion etch in 200 mm MEMS fabs cuts 100:1 trenches, giving ~100 fF cells (vs ~5 fF today) that hold data ~20x longer for the same leakage.
why: Refresh and supply: long retention allows low-refresh buffer DRAM built in MEMS capacity outside the memory oligopoly; density is low, so it targets refresh-light buffer roles, not bulk bits.

title: Substitute CVD tungsten lines with electroplated copper in memory tiers
idea: Swap WF6-based tungsten wordlines and bitlines in BEOL memory tiers for electroplated copper with ALD barriers at <=400 C, using U.S.-sourced copper and the logic BEOL plating supply chain.
why: Removes China-dominated tungsten and WF6 from memory tiers and gives ~3x lower line resistance for longer, cheaper arrays.

title: Coulomb-blockade charge sensors let mature 28 nm logic fabs build DRAM
idea: Replace the bitline sense amp with a room-temperature silicon-nanowire single-electron transistor whose few-nm dot (formed by oxidation pinch-off) resolves a few hundred electrons. A 0.3-0.5 fF planar MIM capacitor then suffices, so the whole cell fits a standard 28 nm logic flow in underused U.S. foundries.
why: Sidesteps the 5 fF capacitor charge wall and turns idle logic capacity into DRAM-class supply at a fraction of new-fab capital.

title: Argon-free vacuum Czochralski with cold-trap SiO capture
idea: Shift the puller's gas regime from argon sweep to molecular flow: grow 300 mm ingots under high vacuum, or in a hydrogen/nitrogen ambient, using large cryo-pumped cold traps and a redesigned heat shield to remove SiO vapor.
why: Crystal growth is a large argon consumer. Ingot supply becomes rare-gas-independent, and crucible life may improve because SiO is removed faster.

title: Blacksmith tempering: high-pressure deuterium re-anneal rescues retention-failed wafers
idea: Smiths re-temper steel to restore toughness. Wafers that fail retention binning at sort, before bumping, get a 20-atm deuterium anneal at 400-450 C that re-passivates interface and junction traps in the access transistors. The weak-cell tail shrinks and the wafers are re-sorted into higher bins.
why: Leakage tail, refresh and yield: if the tail shrinks even 2x, 1-3% of wafers and many low bins are recovered. High-pressure anneal furnaces exist in nanofabs.

title: Open DRAM PDK and cell library for mature 300mm fabs
idea: Fuse the open-source silicon movement (SkyWater/GF open PDKs, RISC-V) with DRAM: publish a royalty-free 1T1C or 2T0C cell, sense-amp, row decoder and DDR-PHY reference design tuned to 28-45 nm logic-compatible flows, so any foundry can tape out commodity-class memory.
why: Breaks the design-IP moat. It lets idle mature-node capacity (U.S., EU, India) supply legacy and edge DRAM and could add several percent of global bits.

title: Helium-free fabs via hydrogen-neon backside cooling and recapture membranes
idea: Inverts 'wafer chucks and leak checks need helium': retrofit electrostatic chucks in etch/CVD tools to run closed-loop low-pressure hydrogen or neon backside gas, and recover residual helium from tool exhaust with on-site membrane purifiers.
why: Scarce resource: Qatar's ~30% helium share is offline; cutting fab helium purchases >90% removes a supply-stop risk for every DRAM line.

title: Synaptic-spine gain cells: every mature logic fab becomes memory fab
idea: Synapses store weight as charge on a dendritic spine with no dedicated capacitor. A 3-transistor silicon gain cell stores charge on the read transistor's gate and ships as an open memory compiler for 28-65 nm logic processes, so U.S. mature logic fabs can make DRAM-class chips with no high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch.
why: Removes the hardest capacitor steps and EUV; widens DRAM-capable U.S. sites from ~1 to >10, at lower density per die.

title: Error-Tolerant DRAM grade: JEDEC spec permitting 1% raw cell errors
idea: Inverts 'every bit must work as shipped': a new JEDEC grade allows up to 1% faulty cells, with a boot-time defect map plus stuck-at masking codes for static faults and a rate-0.85 LDPC for random ones in the controller, sold as a cheaper price tier.
why: Cost per bit and supply: die now binned out for tiny fault counts become saleable; static faults cost only ~1-3% overhead with known-location coding, so good bits per wafer may rise 10-25%.

title: Oil infill drilling: recover wafer-edge DRAM die with partial fields
idea: Adapted from infill drilling that taps oil left between existing wells: tape out a half-size 'edge die' variant and a step map that fills the partial-field ring and narrows edge exclusion, using reticle blading and tighter bevel-etch and edge-bead control.
why: The edge ring wastes ~5-10% of gross 300 mm area; recovering a third of it adds ~2-3% bits per wafer at near-zero capex (cost per bit).

title: DNA-brick templates position contact holes at 15 nm pitch
idea: Po: DNA draws the circuit. DNA-brick crystals self-assemble onto DUV-defined binding sites carrying metal-oxide precursors, which are converted into a hard mask for contact or capacitor holes at ~15 nm pitch; the DNA is burned off before high-temperature steps.
why: Benchtop self-assembly gives sub-EUV feature placement; attacks capital intensity, though placement error and contamination are speculative.

title: KV-cache card that decays precision of aging tokens
idea: Extreme user: million-token-context AI. A 10-person team builds an FPGA CXL card that holds fresh KV entries at FP8 and requantizes entries older than N tokens to FP4, then 2-bit, in place, repacking pages to free capacity without host involvement.
why: 2-3x effective KV capacity per GB, relieving HBM and DDR demand.

title: Right-to-repair mandate: socketed memory in laptops and servers
idea: Ideal: memory outlives the device it ships in. Closest achievable with no new fab: regulation requires CAMM2/SO-DIMM-style socketed memory in PCs and modular memory in servers, with standard reuse labels, so DRAM is harvested whole at end of life instead of shredded with the board.
why: Reuse: recoverable DRAM from retired PCs rises from <5% to >50%.

title: Block copolymer DSA plus infiltration synthesis for honeycomb capacitors
idea: Combine PS-b-PMMA cylinder-forming block copolymer (hexagonal, matching DRAM's honeycomb capacitor layout) with sequential infiltration synthesis of Al2O3 into PMMA to make a hard mask, followed by BCl3/Cl2 transfer etch. There is no fluorine at any step.
why: Self-assembles the densest DRAM array layer without EUV or fluorocarbon etch, cutting a 5-7 EUV-layer bill.

title: Sleep-consolidation fleet program migrating cold pages off DRAM nightly
idea: During sleep the brain moves memories from hippocampus to cortex. A fleet-wide scheduled job moves pages untouched for hours to compressed or CXL-flash tiers during low load, then shrinks VM DRAM reservations to measured working sets.
why: Working sets are often 30-50% of allocated DRAM; reclaiming 20% fleetwide equals years of new fab output.

title: Franchise recipe book: one certified memory process for every university fab
idea: Franchises win with an exact operations manual. Freeze an open 'franchise' process for a memory test vehicle, an oxide-channel 1T1C/2T0C array on 150/200 mm using i-line, ALD and sputter, with fixed recipes, golden wafers and inline metrics. Participating nanofabs certify on it and swap wafers mid-flow.
why: Strategy and time: creates a distributed U.S. memory pilot-line network with interchangeable data that speeds materials and cell qualification, at ~$1-2M per site.

title: Wallpaper: roll-to-roll fine-line polyimide interposers for HBM
idea: Random stimulus 'wallpaper' -> patterned rolls laminated onto walls. Roll-to-roll semi-additive copper on 25 um polyimide at 2/2 um L/S (flex-display-style R2R photolithography) is laminated on a glass stiffener as the HBM-to-GPU interposer.
why: Bypasses the silicon-interposer bottleneck; interposer cost est. 5-10x lower and capacity scales with web lines not 300 mm fabs, so more HBM ships per year.

title: Eliminate RMA scrapping: bad-row map stored in module SPD
idea: Eliminate discarding DIMMs with a few failing rows: an open firmware/Linux patch learns failing rows from correctable-error telemetry and writes a compact retirement map into spare SPD EEPROM bytes, so every future host offlines those pages; ~$300k, 12 months, upstreamed to Linux and coreboot.
why: Most fleet DIMM replacements (~1-3%/year) are few-row faults; keeping them in service saves petabytes per hyperscaler.

title: Li: Lithium-niobate photonics wafer lines make domain-wall memory
idea: Thin-film LiNbO3-on-insulator wafers, now mass-produced for modulators, host ferroelectric domain-wall memory where a written conducting wall bridges two electrodes and is read nondestructively in nanoseconds.
why: Non-volatile, nondestructive read and high endurance, reusing a fast-growing wafer supply chain.

title: Forming-gas hydrogen tracer replaces helium leak checking fleet-wide
idea: Time-and-scale shift of a maintenance routine: every vacuum tool and gas line in the fab is leak-checked with 5% H2/N2 forming gas and networked MEMS hydrogen sensors that log trends continuously instead of once per shift.
why: Leak checking is a top helium sink. This saves ~10-20% of fab helium, and continuous monitoring catches leaks days earlier.

title: Mapper's throughput death fixed: e-beam writes only cuts on gratings
idea: Mapper's massively multi-beam e-beam lithography went bankrupt in 2018 because writing whole layers was too slow (~10 wafers per hour). Fix: use multibeam only for the sparse cuts and contact holes on top of self-aligned quadruple-patterned gratings (DRAM arrays are highly periodic), so the beams expose ~1-2% of the area and effective throughput rises ~50x.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital: replaces 2-4 of DRAM's EUV layers with tools costing a fraction of a $200M scanner, ending single-supplier lock-in for those layers.

title: Minify temperature to 77 K: capacitorless cryogenic memory vaults
idea: At 77 K junction and subthreshold leakage collapse by orders of magnitude, so a deposited poly-Si 1T0C cell (no capacitor, no EUV) holds data for hours; stack ~100 such layers and run racks in liquid-nitrogen baths costing cents per liter.
why: Removes the capacitor charge wall and refresh; cheap stacked poly-Si layers target ~$0.1/GB (~100x), trading cooling energy and system complexity.

title: Resell retention-reject die as 1%-tolerant memory instead of scrapping
idea: Inverts 'a die that fails 64 ms retention is scrap': die whose weak-cell tail is too long for standard refresh go to controllers that map and code around up to 1% leaky cells while keeping the normal refresh rate.
why: Yield and cost: retention is a top fallout mode at 1a/1b nodes; recovering those die adds a few percent of bits per wafer at near-zero cost.

title: Substitute megafabs with containerized low-temperature memory lines
idea: Swap $15B megafabs for ISO-container tool modules (sputter, spatial ALD, imprint, plating, metrology), possible because <=400 C flows need no diffusion furnaces or implanters, set up next to data centers.
why: Distributed U.S. manufacturing in modules of ~$50-100M, deployed in months; capacity scales with demand rather than in decade-long steps.

title: Expired-patent DRAM: litigation-free process from public-domain IP
idea: Turn the patent wall into a commons: mine DRAM patents filed before ~2006 (now expired), covering stacked and trench capacitors, recessed-channel transistors and 6F2 layouts. Build a royalty-free 30-40 nm-class flow from them, staffed by former Elpida, Qimonda and Inotera engineers.
why: U.S. manufacturability: removes newcomers' biggest legal risk. On used tools, the flow delivers capacity-tier bits fast.

title: Every failed die must ship: salvage-grade DRAM with controller sparing
idea: Self-imposed limit: no die is scrapped. Fabs sell dies that fail speed or have more bad rows than fuse repair covers as a 'salvage grade'; a host or CXL controller with large row-remap tables and spare-die striping uses them for KV-cache and cold tiers that tolerate lower speed.
why: Recovers part of the 10-20% wafer yield fallout as usable bits; +3-8% effective supply with no new capex.

title: Laser-modified glass interposers relieve the HBM packaging bottleneck
idea: Femtosecond pulses locally change glass so it etches ~100x faster in HF (laser-induced deep etching), giving dense through-glass vias in panel-size glass cores. HBM-to-GPU interposers get made on panel lines instead of scarce 65 nm silicon interposer capacity.
why: HBM output is gated by interposer/advanced packaging; panel glass gives ~5x more area per substrate at lower cost.

title: Reconstituted known-good-die wafers before hybrid-bonded HBM stacking
idea: Worse: bond whole wafers so one bad die poisons a 12-high stack. Flip: dice and test each core die, place only known-good dies into reconstituted 300 mm carrier wafers fan-out style, then hybrid-bond the reconstituted wafers wafer-to-wafer for throughput.
why: Attacks the HBM yield tax (20-30% loss): stack yield approaches single-die yield, recovering ~15-25% of HBM bits.

title: Thermal atomic-layer etch for capacitor-hole and recess steps
idea: Time shift from continuous plasma etch to self-limiting second-scale chemical cycles (fluorination, then ligand exchange): critical recess and trim etches remove one atomic layer per cycle, with no plasma and no argon dilution.
why: Removes argon from the precision etch steps and gives Angstrom control of wordline recess depth, which tightens the leakage tail. Tool capex is ~30% lower than high-density plasma.

title: Open DRAM reference PDK lets logic foundries enter commodity memory
idea: DRAM's moat is accumulated know-how, not physics: periphery is ~49% of the die and is ordinary CMOS. Fund an open reference design (cell, sense amp, redundancy, test) plus an open 1x-nm process recipe for licensed U.S. foundries, backed by an indemnified shared patent pool.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply diversity: lowers entry from ~$15B plus a decade of learning to a foundry add-on module, breaking the three-vendor oligopoly.
